text.text: Experts have described 575,748 proteins by hand, only 0.91% of them from ocean animals, and the two standard checks name no function for 19.4% of a Pacific oyster's proteins.

Figure 1. Every protein of two animals, one tile each. Like Earth seen from space at night, lit tiles show where knowledge reaches; ocean animals are the dark continents. Hover or tap a tile to see the protein. UniProt 2026_03 reference proteomes, one protein per gene: human UP000005640, oyster UP000005408.

This site measures, for every tool and every kind of organism, which proteins get a label and what the run costs, and tells each lab which tool to run. The first organism page will be the Pacific oyster's; it is not built yet, so there is no link to it.
Why ocean animals are dark
Science describes proteins where people work on them. Five species hold more reviewed proteins than all ocean animals put together, many times over.

Figure 2. The five best-studied species hold 90,318 reviewed proteins (15.7% of all), about 18,064 each. The 880 ocean animal species hold 5,257 together, 6.0 each. The other 10,885 species hold 480,114. 59 entries have no species and are left out. Source: Swiss-Prot, UniProt 2026_03 (02-Sep-2026); World Register of Marine Species habitat flags.
Mussel foot protein Mytilus edulis, Blue mussel, Q25460
Blue mussels use it to glue their threads to wet rock. Its repeated 10-residue stretches carry DOPA, a modified tyrosine, and chemists copy that chemistry to make glues that set under water.
A tool labels it today.

MMseqs2 against Swiss-Prot: 2 other Swiss-Prot proteins at least 30% identical; the closest, Q27409, is 71% identical over residues 1-859

Fish antifreeze glycoprotein Notothenia neglecta, Yellowbelly rockcod, P24856

Antarctic rockcod make it to keep their blood from freezing in sea water below 0 °C. The chain is cut into 46 short glycopeptides, nearly all repeats of Ala-Ala-Thr, that stop ice crystals from growing.
No tool here labels it today.

Cone snail toxin (omega-conotoxin MVIIA) Conus magus, Magical cone, P05484
The 25-residue toxin of a cone snail is the painkiller ziconotide (sold as Prialt), given to patients whom opiates no longer help.
A tool labels it today.

Green fluorescent protein (GFP) Aequorea victoria, Water jellyfish, P42212
A jellyfish protein that glows green. Labs worldwide fuse it to other proteins to watch them inside living cells; its discovery and development won the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

Figure 3. Four ocean proteins that changed medicine and biology, and what the tools find on them today. Residues and features: UniProt 2026_03. Matches: InterPro API and MMseqs2 against Swiss-Prot (Prompt E, step 6).

The proteins that gave us underwater glue, antifreeze, a painkiller and the green light of cell biology were all found at the bench, by people, not by a tool. Three of the four are built from repeats or short peptides. On the leaderboard, the best tool finds 7 in 100 known features 2 to 15 residues long, against 28 in 100 features of any length. Repeats are found about as often as other features (30 in 100), and stretches with no fixed shape are not yet measured.

For scale: CAFA, the Critical Assessment of protein Function Annotation, has run as a community challenge since 2010. Open Problems (Luecken et al., Nature Biotechnology 2025, co-authored by Olga Botvinnik) does the same for single-cell analysis tools.
Who is behind it
Seanome Inc., a nonprofit.
The maintainers of nf-core/proteinannotator, the pipeline that labels a proteome's proteins.
If the proposed fork goes ahead (nothing agreed yet): the LAFA / CAFA group, who run functionbench.net (source).
Licence: the site's own repository has no licence file yet. Each tool keeps its own licence, listed on its tool card.
Contact: open an issue at github.com/seanome/protein-function-annotation-leaderboard/issues, or write to info@seanome.org.
